Evanson Former Vice President of Investor Relations Thank you, Patrick, and good afternoon, everyone. Welcome to our first quarter financial results question- and-answer conference call. The shareholder letter, financial results and webcast of this Q&A session are all available at our Investor Relations website at ir.teslamotors.com. Today's call is for your questions, and we will conduct the Q&A session live. [Operator Instructions] Like last quarter, we will limit this call to 45 minutes. During the course of this call, we may discuss our business outlook and make forward-looking statements. Such statements are predictions based on management's current expectations. Benjamin Schuman Pacific Crest Securities, Inc., Research Division My first question is around the ZEV credits. You disclosed the amount of revenue in Q1. Can you say how much is implied in the Q2 gross margin guidance? And kind of as part of that, what are some of the big gross margin drivers to get from that 5% level now, excluding the ZEV revenue, to 25%? And do you expect that 25% also without whatever positive impact from the lease accounting that you might see? Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Okay. Looks like a few questions nested in there. Yes, so we are expecting a decline in ZEV credit revenue for Q2, and then probably a fairly significant decline in Q3. And as I said, like right now, we're not expecting anything in Q4. But that's not to say that -- I mean, there might be some ZEV credit revenue in Q4, but we're not counting on it. I don't know. I can't give anymore precision than that at this time. But I think sort of -- Benjamin Schuman Pacific Crest Securities, Inc., Research Division Okay, so bigger decline in Q3 than in Q2; is it fair to say that? Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Oh, sure, of course, yes. Benjamin Schuman Pacific Crest Securities, Inc., Research Division Okay. And then just one more for me. The $200 million in CapEx, can you talk about just what that's going to, exactly. Maybe how much of the gross margin improvement might be tied to additional capital expenditures? Deepak Ahuja Former Chief Financial Officer Ben, Deepak here. Clearly, some of the CapEx is related to improvements we're making in-house by bringing more equipment in and automating our processes that will result in gross margin improvement. And a portion of that is also new product development, and then another portion is the infrastructure development of our service centers, our stores and the Supercharger network. Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Yes. I think -- and it's worth noting that -- and we were profitable in Q1, despite actually spending quite a lot of money on new service centers, expanding the Supercharger network stores and other things that obviously we won't need to keep doing -- I mean, that's something that's going to need to occur on an ongoing basis, but we need to establish a service network in particular for example. Operator The next question comes from Dan Galves with Deutsche Bank. Daniel V. Galves TESLA, INC. FQ1 2013 EARNINGS CALL | MAY 08, 2013 Copyright © 2019 S&P Global Market Intelligence, a division of S&P Global Inc. All Rights reserved. spglobal.com/marketintelligence 6 Deutsche Bank AG, Research Division First one, again, kind of regarding the gross margin. I did the -- I think the same simple math that Ben did to get to somewhere in the 5% to 6% gross margin, automotive gross margin, excluding the ZEV credits. If that's in the ballpark, it seems like you need to increase gross profit per unit by something in the $17,000 to $19,000 per unit by the end of the year. Wondering if you could give us kind of the big buckets that you're targeting for that improvement? And how much is within your control and how much might be -- you might need price concessions from your suppliers, if any? Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Sure. Well, first, it's worth noting that when you see the gross margin for Q1, we're giving you the, obviously, the gross margin average over the quarter. And so the gross margin at the end of Q1 was significantly better than at the beginning of Q1. So you may sort of think that we're starting from a base of 5% or 6%, but actually we're starting from a base that's a bit better than that. And then in terms of where the additional cost savings are coming from, it's a wide range of activities. Most of these have been put in place either in Q4 last year or in Q1, but it takes time for those actions to bear fruit. They don't happen instantly. And it's sort of -- like this wire rate, it's improving the cost of our logistics, improving -- you're getting better deals from suppliers. Design improvements -- design improvements are the ones that take the longest to come to fruition, which is why we're only confident of the 25% gross margin number in Q4, not sooner; it's because there are a number of improvements that are designed-related so you've got to finish the design, you've got to validate it and then put it into production. So... Deepak Ahuja Former Chief Financial Officer And I'll add to that, manufacturing process improvements both in-house and at our suppliers, it takes costs out. Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Yes, yes. I mean, a number of those product suppliers have really done some impressive work on cost reduction. And for some others, they just didn't believe that we'd do these numbers, so they didn't quite tool up for this level of production. Their internal predictions were that we would do in some cases 3,000 over the entire lifetime of the product. I'm like, "Yes, we did that last quarter." So as they sort of come to believe that those things, that these projections are real, then they actually tool up and are able to deliver significant cost savings for our part supply. Daniel V. Galves Deutsche Bank AG, Research Division Okay, got you. So just a follow-up. The suppliers are cooperating with you in terms of reducing. So I guess, are you still experiencing a lot of premium freight from suppliers that weren't ready to produce that volume? Are they cooperating with you in terms of the design improvements and kind of redesigning the component? And then my second question relates to cash flow. What's causing the decline from 65 million of OCF in Q1 to the guidance of neutral in Q2? And if you could remind us of your minimum cash level. Deepak Ahuja Former Chief Financial Officer So to answer your first question, our expedited freight is continuing to reduce every month that goes by, as both our suppliers have additional capacity to meet our needs and our production schedule is becoming much more stable. So it's all trending in the right direction. And then to that same point of Elon, where we ended with our freight costs at the end of Q1 was better than the average for the quarter. So it gives us comfort that -- or confidence that we'll continue to reduce our cost. And then in terms of our cash flows, we are mindful of the volumes. As you can see, we are projecting lower deliveries in North America, since we have quite a few cars on the board being shipped to Europe. And that consumes some degree of TESLA, INC. Operator The next question comes from Aditya Satghare with Lazard capital markets. Aditya A. Satghare Lazard Capital Markets LLC, Research Division I had 2. First is on the manufacturing process. You talked about the number of manufacturing hours being reduced by 40%. Can you give us a sense of how much more room is there to grow, and where does that stand in relation to your target? And then I have a follow-up. Deepak Ahuja Former Chief Financial Officer I think there's clearly room to grow further, and there are a lot of activities in our manufacturing organization that are continuing in that direction. And then towards the second half of the year, as we start to increase our production rate slightly further than our present level, that will further add to the labor reduction on a core unit basis. Aditya A. Satghare Lazard Capital Markets LLC, Research Division Got it. Second question on demand. When you talk about the 15,000 units per year, does that include both sort of the cash and lease demand? And would you also give us some more color on when we think about the 15,000 non-U.S. units, what geographies do you expect that demand to come from? And maybe a little bit more color on the buyer base, who potentially could be buying these cars? Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Yes, we actually expect probably most of our purchasers long-term will be financed purchasers, which is actually normal for premium sedans. Most -- the majority are financed. And in fact, in our case, it might have been a supermajority because the best way to appreciate the savings you get from gasoline is to look at it in on a monthly basis. In the U.S., you maybe save $200 to $300 a month in gasoline relative to electricity costs, if it's your daily driver. In Europe, obviously, that number can be doubled. It can be maybe $500 a month, and -- if you're driving here, because the cost of gasoline is twice as much. So I think -- given that, I think we'll see over time, my guess is that it'll be a supermajority financed in one form or another. And I believe that also opens up the potential, the affordability of the car to a much broader -- a much larger number of people. And I think, if our car was exclusively available for purchase and not by financing, I think that's maybe accessible to 1% or roughly 1 million U.S. households. As a financed product with the right financing -- sort of fully optimized finance product, I think it's probably accessible to the top 10 million households. And then it, of course, depends on what percentage of those households who want to buy our car versus somebody else's. But I do think that it's -- yes, long term, it's primarily a finance product. Aditya A. Satghare Lazard Capital Markets LLC, Research Division And could you touch on sort of non-U.S. demand in terms of geographical mix and where it comes from? Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Yes, sure. Well, I think we'll see probably at least 10,000 units a year from demand in Europe and then at least 5,000 in Asia. But I mean, that could be, obviously, a much bigger number. China is kind of a TESLA, INC. Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Sure. So we don't have any plans right now to raise funding. And just a follow-up to an earlier question about the geographic split. Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Well, I think, obviously, given that the first half of year is entirely North America, that obviously puts the floor at 10,000. If we stop shipping to America on July 1, then we would still have something like 10,000 North American cars. So we're obviously not going to do that. So we're -- it's probably -- but do not take these numbers as final in any way, but you just have -- if I'm asked to sort of speculate, I mean, it's probably something like 15,000 in North America, and 5,000 in Europe and 1,000 in Asia. But this is -- yes, don't hold me to these numbers, I just want to -- if it stays up, I want it bracket it with the appropriate confidence interval. That's my best guess. I mean, is there any kind of feeling of probability that you can give us that would allow us to sort of handicap that? Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect I think, I would realistically handicap it at 0 for the fourth quarter. Which is less -- I mean, we'll sell it if we can. But honestly, we'd anticipate saturating demand for ZEV credits probably in the third quarter. So maybe that's not true, but I wouldn't -- for purposes of modeling our financials, I would recommend assuming 0 for ZEV credits in the Q4. Operator TESLA, INC.
